theme: From the horns of the wild oxen you have rescued me
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 22. You have read parts of this psalm twice before in earlier units. Read it again now with Isaiah 53 open beside it. Both describe a righteous sufferer who is forsaken, pierced, and then vindicated, so that the nations turn to the LORD.
settingTheScene: Psalm 22 is a psalm of David, and the Gospels show Jesus praying its first line from the cross. Paired with the fourth Servant Song, it shows the suffering and glory that the Old Testament predicts for the Messiah. Notice especially the second half, in which the sufferer is delivered and the result is worldwide worship. That is the same pattern as Isaiah 53:10-12.
observation: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me?” (v. 1).
“But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people” (v. 6).
“All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads” (v. 7).
“They have pierced my hands and feet” (v. 16).
“They divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots” (v. 18).
“You who fear the LORD, praise him! … For he has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted” (vv. 23-24).
“All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations shall worship before you” (v. 27).
“They shall come and proclaim his righteousness to a people yet unborn, that he has done it” (v. 31).
interpretation:
Read beside Isaiah 53, the psalm reveals the same shape. The Servant is despised and rejected, and the psalmist is “a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind.” The Servant is silent before his accusers, and the psalmist is surrounded by bulls, lions, and dogs. The Servant is pierced and crushed, and the psalmist’s bones are out of joint, his heart like wax, his strength dried up. Even his clothes are divided. And then in both, the turn.

In Isaiah 53:10-11, “he shall see his offspring; he shall prolong his days… out of the anguish of his soul he shall see and be satisfied.” In Psalm 22:21-22, the sufferer is heard and begins to declare God’s name to his brothers and praise him in the congregation. The suffering was not the end.

Verses 24 to 31 are the surprising conclusion. God “has not despised or abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, and he has not hidden his face from him, but has heard, when he cried to him.” The cry of dereliction is answered. And its effect is global: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD.” The affliction of one man brings all nations to worship. “The poor shall eat and be satisfied.” Compare Isaiah 53:11, “make many to be accounted righteous,” and Isaiah 49:6, a light for the nations.

The psalm ends with the future generations: “They shall come and proclaim his righteousness to a people yet unborn, that he has done it.” The Hebrew for “that he has done it” is a single word, much like Jesus’ cry, “It is finished.”

Why is it here? Because Isaiah’s Servant is not an abstract idea. Real suffering is involved, in real flesh. The psalm gives the Servant a voice. It shows what he felt: abandonment, mockery, thirst, and yet, trust, and ultimately praise. Because of this, Christians in suffering have a companion in the one who prayed this psalm to the end.
connection: Jesus cried, “Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani” on the cross (Matthew 27:46), and the details of Psalm 22 are found throughout the passion narratives: mocking (Matthew 27:39-43), the dividing of garments (John 19:23-24), thirst (John 19:28). Hebrews 2:12 puts verse 22 on Jesus’ lips. Revelation 7:9 shows people from all nations worshiping. John 19:30 records “It is finished.” Romans 8:34 says Christ is at the right hand of God, interceding.
application:
Read the psalm aloud as Jesus’ prayer. Thank him for walking through abandonment so that you never have to be abandoned.

If you feel forsaken, pray verse 1 honestly, and then continue reading to verse 24.

Pray for a nation or people group that has not heard the gospel, using verse 27.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he did not despise the affliction of his Son.
Thank Jesus for crying out in forsakenness for you.
Ask him to make you tell others of what he has done.
